I would first take a sample of a few hundred answers, have people rate them with the same rubric the judge uses, and measure how often the judge agrees with the human ratings. I would give the judge a clear rubric and reference answers where possible. Then I would watch for known biases: preferring longer answers, preferring whichever answer is shown first, and preferring answers written in its own style. The tradeoff is human review cost, so I would keep a smaller human sample running over time and recheck the judge whenever the prompt or model changes.

I would build pairs of answers with the same content where one is padded to be much longer, and check whether the judge scores the longer one higher. I would also swap the order of answers in pairwise comparisons and measure how often the verdict flips. If length or order changes the score, I would adjust the rubric or normalize for it and confirm against human ratings.

Benchmark contamination means the benchmark questions, or close copies, appeared in the model's training data, so the score measures memorization rather than ability. Public benchmarks may also not resemble our tasks at all. For our use case I would build a private evaluation set from real internal tasks, run every candidate model with the same prompts and settings, and compare quality, latency, and cost. I would keep that set private so it does not leak into future training data.

I would include common real requests sampled from logs with personal data removed, hard cases where past systems failed, out-of-scope requests the model should decline, and a few risky requests to check safety. Each example would have a defined good answer or rubric, and I would add new failures from production every month.

In one project I owned a support assistant built on retrieval. During error analysis I found that answer quality had dropped after we changed how documents were split into chunks, because tables were being cut in half. I measured the impact on our evaluation set, rolled back the chunking change, fixed the splitter to keep tables whole, and verified the fix on the regression set before shipping it again.

I told my lead and the support team the same day, with the numbers from the evaluation and the rollback plan, and posted a short write-up in our team channel. Afterwards I added the failing cases to our regression tests so any future chunking change is checked against them automatically.
